en: The Buddha Spoke the Sūtra on Jyotiṣka, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Khotan during the Song Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "In the past, there was a great wealthy householder named Jyotiṣka, whose granaries and treasuries were full to overflowing."
He was fully endowed with gold and silver, and his retinue of male and female servants was complete without any deficiency.
There was a white cotton hand-towel hanging by the side of a pond, which, encountering a rising wind from the heavens, was blown before the king’s palace.
The king immediately convened a great assembly of his ministers to deliberate together; they arranged divinations and inquiries, marveling at the cause of these omens.
All the ministers said, "The kingdom is about to experience great prosperity, for Heaven has bestowed upon us this white cotton cloth."
Jyotiṣka remained silent and spoke no word.
The king asked Jyotiṣka, "All the ministers are joyful; why do you remain silent?"
Tiga replied, "I dare not deceive Your Majesty!
This is a towel for wiping the body belonging to my household, which was hanging by the side of the pond when a celestial wind arose and blew it before Your Majesty’s palace."
"For this reason, I remained silent and spoke no word.
After several days had passed, a nine-colored golden flower, as large as a chariot wheel, was encountered by a celestial wind that blew it before the king's palace.
The king immediately convened a great assembly of his ministers to deliberate together, arranging divinations and inquiries to investigate the cause of this marvel.
All the ministers said, "The kingdom is about to flourish greatly; Heaven has bestowed upon us these golden flowers."
The minister Jotika remained silent and spoke no word.
The king asked Jotika, "All the ministers are joyful; why do you remain silent?"
Ti-ga replied, "I dare not deceive Your Majesty!
These are withered flowers from the rear garden of my household that, encountering a rising celestial wind, were blown before Your Majesty’s palace."
"For this reason, I remain silent and say nothing.
The King asked Ti-ga:
"Is it truly so in your family?"
"Make preparations quickly; I wish to lead twenty thousand followers to your residence to pay you a visit.
Jyotiṣka replied, "I pray that Your Majesty will accompany me to my home.

I possess beds and mats that appear spontaneously and require no one to spread them; food and drink that appear spontaneously and require no one to prepare; things brought forth spontaneously without the need for calling out; and things taken away spontaneously without the need to look back."
The king immediately led a multitude of two hundred thousand people to visit and tour the house of Jyotiṣka.

Entering directly through the southern gate, they encountered a young boy at the entrance; his countenance was upright and handsome, his complexion was radiant and pleasing, and he was most endearing to behold.
The King asked Jyotiṣka,
"Is this the son or grandson of your family? Jyotiṣka replied:
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty!
This is a slave who guards the gate of my household.
He advanced a short distance further to the middle gate, where there was a young girl whose countenance was upright and whose complexion was radiant and pleasing; she was exceedingly lovely.
The king asked Jyotiṣka,
"Is this a woman from your household? Jyotiṣka replied:
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty! She is a maidservant who guards the gatehouse of my household.

He advanced a short distance further into the chamber; the walls were of white silver and the floor was of crystal. When the King called out for the water to flow, [the servant] hesitated and could not proceed. Jyotiṣka then led the King forward and inside; there was a bed of gold and a table of white jade, and Jyotiṣka’s wife had one hundred and twenty sets of precious gold and silver curtains and canopies.
Jyotiṣka’s wife was peerlessly beautiful; as she paid homage to the king, tears fell from her eyes.
The king asked Jyotiṣka, "When your wife saw me, what was so unpleasant that tears fell from her eyes?"
Tiga replied, “I dare not deceive Your Majesty!
It was because I caught the scent of Your Majesty’s smoke that tears welled up in my eyes.”
The King said:
"Commoners burn fat, feudal lords burn wax, and the Son of Heaven burns lac; none of these produce smoke, so how could they possibly yield tears?"
Tiga replied, “I dare not deceive Your Majesty!

In my household, there is a divine moon-pearl suspended in the hall; it remains unchanged day and night, requiring no firelight. Since Your Majesty is the King of Scents, you have merely smelled its fragrance.”

In front of the hall of Jyotiṣka’s house was a twelve-story high tower; the king was led up to its top, where he gazed toward the east and forgot the west, and gazed toward the south and forgot the north, remaining there in a state of languid stupor for an entire month.
The minister said, "State affairs are of great importance; we must return to settle and govern the people.
The king replied:
"In a short while, it will become slightly more bearable.

Jyotiṣka then led the king to wander and view the rear garden, where they bathed in flowing springs and bathing pools, ate fruits that were incomparably sweet and delicious, and found great delight therein for as long as one month.
The minister said to the king:
"It is necessary to return to the kingdom; the affairs of state are of great importance, and the people must be governed.
The king replied:
"Alas! In a brief moment, it may yet become bearable.
Sudatta immediately bestowed gold, silver, rare treasures, and silken brocades; then two hundred thousand people, along with their horses and carriages, all returned to the kingdom together.
The king immediately assembled his ministers to sit together in consultation, arranging divinations and inquiries while marveling at the cause:
"Jyotiṣka is my minister, yet his women and dwellings exceed my own in abundance."
"I wish to attack him; can he be captured or not?
All the ministers replied, "It would be appropriate to capture him."
The king immediately mobilized a multitude of four hundred thousand men, beating gongs and sounding drums, and went to surround Jyotiṣka’s house in more than several hundred layers.

At the gate of Jyotiṣka’s house stood a strongman who, seizing a golden staff and brandishing it but once, caused the entire multitude of four hundred thousand to fall down all at once; their limbs twisted and contorted, their buttocks and loins wrenched, appearing like those intoxicated, with heads shaking and hair disheveled, they lay on the ground unable to rise.
Jyotiṣka, riding in a flying cloud-chariot, asked the people from within the void of space:
"What was your intention when you came, that you lie upon the ground and do not rise?
The people answered Jyotiṣka, saying:
"The king has sent me here, intending to attack the elder.

Within the elder's gate there is a powerful man who, with a single brandish of his golden staff, caused our entire host of four hundred thousand to fall down all at once, lying on the ground unable to rise."
Jyotiṣka asked them, "Would you like to attain it?
and all the people replied:
"I wish for you all to rise.
Sudarśana cast a glance with his great divine eye, and the assembly of four hundred thousand people rose simultaneously and returned to their own country.

The king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Jyotiṣka. Jyotiṣka traveled together with the king in the same carriage; they proceeded to the place where the Buddha was staying, and the king asked:
"World-Honored One!..."
“Jyotiṣka was my minister; what meritorious deeds did he perform in his previous lives that his women and palace now surpass mine?
The Buddha said, “By virtue of Jyotiṣka’s merit from practicing generosity, he currently enjoys happiness in the heavens.”

In the past, five hundred caravan leaders, leading their merchants and carrying precious treasures, were traveling through a perilous road when they entered a desolate mountain. There they encountered a sick practitioner; they provided him with a thatched hut and thick bedding, supplied him with water, broth, cooking utensils, and grain, and gave him lamps and candles. At that time, he made a vow for the reward of rebirth in heaven, and now he has obtained the fruit of that retribution.
The Buddha said:
“The donor at that time was none other than the husband and wife Jyotiṣka;
the sick practitioner at that time was my own self.”
"The five hundred caravan leaders and merchants have all attained the path of Arhatship.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Jyotiṣka Sūtra*.
